results.fact: Day-1 gain to Upper Royal Basin
results.evidence: Real: 1,800 ft is too low. A 2017 party's GPS gave 3,600 ft gain (10.7 mi) for the hike-in day to Upper Royal Lake at 5,720 ft, and the park gives 2,550 to 5,100 ft to Royal Lake alone. But no source gives a car-to-car gain for Johnson alone (the 2017 summit day combined Clark and Johnson: 3,760 ft), so raising Day 1 would push the itinerary total well past gain_ft 5,180 without a sourced total to match. Settle with a sourced Johnson-only car-to-car gain.

results.correct_value: The route finishes up the rightmost chimney (class 4) on the summit block, reached by a ledge south from the lower snowfield, the upper snowfield and a gully behind Sweat Spire and Gasp Pinnacle; descent reverses it.
results.evidence: The fresh pitch_detail already describes the rightmost-chimney finish; the itinerary and descent still describe a SE-ridge gully off a corkscrew ledge. Resolved together with the discovered corkscrew finding below (same patches): two independent trip reports (2009, 2017) and a 2019 report all finish Johnson via the summit-block chimney.

results.fact: Summit route: the row's ledge route is Mount Clark's corkscrew
results.correct_value: Johnson: drop ~100 ft from the Clark-Johnson col, lower snowfield, narrow ledge south to the upper snowfield, gully behind Sweat Spire/Gasp Pinnacle, rightmost class 4 chimney on the summit block. The cairned class 3 crack around a corner with ledges is Mount Clark's route.
results.evidence: A 2017 trip report climbing both peaks from the col describes Clark's route as ledges around a corner with a steep downward class 3 crack, and Johnson's as: drop 100 ft, lower snowfield to its upper-left corner, narrow ledge left to the upper snowfield, then the rightmost chimney on the summit block. A separate 2009 party describes the same ledge south toward the basin below Gasp and Sweat and the summit-block chimney (they used a 5th-class notch variant between the spires). A 2019 report likewise gives class 3 around Gasp Pinnacle then a class 4 chimney. Itinerary day 2, schedule, timing section, descent, the 'Corkscrew ledge crux' waypoint (elevation now unknown), hazards[4] and the approach variant's crack text were Clark's and are rewritten to Johnson's line.

patches.replace: drop about 100 ft and climb Johnson's lower snowfield to its upper-left corner, then take the narrow, exposed ledge south onto the upper snowfield. A loose, low-angle gully and the foot of a low wall lead around behind Sweat Spire and Gasp Pinnacle to the summit block, where the rightmost chimney (class 4) gains the crest just below the top. Reverse the entire route to descend, facing in on the chimney, and re-cross the notch back to camp.

patches.fact: Summit route: the row's ledge route is Mount Clark's corkscrew
patches.find: The ledge system then wraps the south and east of the summit block until it reaches a corner where it looks for all the world as though it cliffs out; a cairned Class 3 crack around that corner is the passage, and missing it in cloud is the recognised crux of the route-finding. Above that a final Class 4 push on loose, rotten rock gains the top. If the rock has gone easy and you are walking broad scree with no ramp above you, you have dropped below the ledge and should climb back to it.
patches.replace: The key passage is a narrow ledge leading left (south) from the top of Johnson's lower snowfield onto the upper snowfield; from there a rubbly gully and the foot of a low wall lead behind the spires to the summit block, where the rightmost of several chimneys is the Class 4 finish on loose, rotten rock. Leaving the upper snowfield too far right puts you in gullies under the spires that steepen into rounded steps and are hard to reverse.
